catalog_locator: §2.5 'Tone', pp.70-71; §5.3 'Tonal Patterns on the Possessive Proclitic', p.127
catalog_quote: 2.5 Tone. Bangime is a tonal language. There are two privative tones, high and low. The tone-bearing unit is the mora. On monosyllabic words with two morae, level tones may combine to form rising or falling melodies. Rising tones may appear on monomoraic syllables in word-initial position. Rising tones on monomoraic words usually appear after a velar consonant. A phonetic mid tone which is the result of a non-automatic downstep predictably appears on the final syllable of a bisyllabic word when the initial syllable is heavy and carries a high tone. ... Most stems in Bangime surface with a pitch change at the syllable or mora break; however, shown in (63), there are exceptions to this generalization. Verbs always surface with a grammatical tone so the generalizations about tonal contrasts are shown mostly on nouns. ... [p.127] The tone of the possessed noun affects the possessive morphem…

new_statements.quote: Bangime is a tonal language. Syllables may be H, L, (H = high tone, L = low tone), rising <LH>, or falling <HL>. Syllables may also be underlyingly toneless <Ø>. Single morae may bear contour tones, but only rising tones. Since only bimoraic syllables may carry falling tones, the tone-bearing unit (TBU) is the syllable. [p. 16] || Any word which is at least bisyllabic with a bimoraic initial syllable causes a syllable with a following high tone to downstep. [...] However, examples such as (24d) 'rain cloud' [ʒɔ̀m̀póǃró] suggest that the issue may be tied to footing, therefore stress could be in fact upstepping the tone of a heavy syllable rather than downstepping a light one. [p. 43; fn. 5: 'Thanks to Stuart Davis for offering this alternative analysis.']

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Bangime has an empty rule and there are no existing stress statements. This work is compatible with that: it establishes that Bangime is tonal with the syllable as TBU and contains no word-stress rule; the one sentence mentioning stress is a speculative alternative to a floating-L downstep analysis (heavy initial syllable possibly upstepped by stress), which could be logged as a weight-related hypothesis but not as a placement rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Bangime is described as a tone language (H, L, rising, falling, and toneless syllables; TBU = syllable; lexical tones frequently overridden by syntactically imposed tone contours). No word-stress placement is stated anywhere. The only mention of stress is a hedged alternative analysis of downstep: a bimoraic (heavy) word-initial syllable in a word of two or more syllables causes downstep of a following H, and the author notes that this 'could be' stress upstepping the heavy syllable's tone instead; this is offered as a possibility credited to Stuart Davis, not as a claim about a stress system.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress (none exists to have exceptions). For the downstep pattern the author gives four examples (dɔ́ɔ́ǃbɛ́ 'short-handled pick-hoe', dúúǃɡú 'forest', mááǃbé 'grass used for making mats', ʒɔ̀m̀póǃró 'rain cloud') and flags 'rain cloud' as the case that motivates the footing/stress alternative.
new_statements.identity_note: The work is a draft descriptive grammar of Bangime, the language isolate of the Bangande villages in Mali; the passages read do not distinguish dialects. Note that the listed open URL (http://dogonlanguages.org/docs/A_Grammar_of_Bangime.pdf) no longer serves the PDF: a live download on 2026-09-18 returned HTTP 200 but redirected to the dogonlanguages.org homepage (144 kB of HTML, saved).

sources.quote: 'Although experiments to determine the language's position along the timing spectrum (mora, syllable, or stress timed) have not yet been performed, a preliminary hypothesis is proposed that the language has meter based on morae.' Later pages contain unedited self-queries ('what if ... other tones were added for stress', 'maybe there must be a high tone (accent!) somewhere on the word?', 'There must be (at most) one high tone on the phrase'). Pre-dissertation musings only; the final 2013 text keeps none of them as a rule.
